title: Dedicated commit flex and blended-rate playbook
content:
Purpose:

This working playbook sketches alternative dedicated commit structures and a blended-rate model intended to make reserved GPU capacity easier to buy for mid-market customers while preserving unit economics. It’s intentionally rough — aim is to capture levers we can test with sales and finance, and the tradeoffs for SRE/infra.

Audience:
- Product + Sales for new pricing experiments
- Finance for commit amortization guidance
- SRE/Capacity planning for predictable utilization assumptions

High-level goals / constraints:
- Provide customers predictable cost per token / req at scale while still giving Redwood room to optimize packing and routing across GPU families.
- Offer simple purchase options for customers who don’t want to manage instance types, plus an advanced option for customers wanting pinned hardware.
- Preserve minimum margin targets (target gross margin on Dedicated = 55% w/ typical packing assumptions).

Key levers explored here (quick list):
1) Commit term length: monthly, quarterly, annual (impact on price per GPU-hour)
2) Burst credits: how much unused commit can be transiently used by other customers via burst pools
3) GPU family mix: allow blended BUYS across A100/RTX/Inferentia-equivalents vs single-family pricing
4) Blended-rate vs SKU-rate: single $/GPU-hour or blended $/vGPU-unit with conversion factor
5) Minimum utilization guarantees and penalties/credits
6) Early termination / ramp protection clauses (discount clawbacks or true-ups)

Simple scenarios (back-of-envelope numbers for discussion):
- Baseline assumptions (internal):
  - A100-equivalent fully-loaded cost (infra amortized + ops): $6.50 / GPU-hour
  - Target Redwood billable price: $12.00 / GPU-hour (55% gross margin target)
  - Typical customer utilization for committed pool: 60% average over month (bursty peaks)
  - Effective tokens per GPU-hour depends on model; assume 100M tokens / hour for medium seq workloads as an anchor

Scenario A: Annual 100% pinned commit (simple SKU pricing)  - Customer pays for N A100-equivalents for 12 months at fixed $/GPU-hour discounted 20% vs on-demand.
  - Pros: simple, predictable for both sides; easy to calculate commit amortization
  - Cons: low packing elasticity, requires overprovisioning by Redwood if utilization low; can increase unit cost if customer use < ~80%
  - Example: list price $12.00 -> committed price $9.60 -> monthly invoice = hours_in_month * N * 9.60

Scenario B: Quarterly blended pool (flex mixing of families)
  - Customer buys a pool expressed in vGPU-units (1 vGPU unit ~ A100-equivalent). Pools can be satisfied by A100, A800, or RTX-based nodes depending on availability. Price is blended across actual GPUs used.
  - Pros: better packing, better chance to hit margin, lower burst latency impact for Redwood
  - Cons: slightly more opaque to customer; needs conversion table and example bill to sell effectively
  - Example: committed blended rate $10.20 / GPU-hour equivalent; Redwood can opportunistically place workloads on lower-cost hardware when safe

Scenario C: Monthly commit + burst credits
  - Customer purchases N committed units per month. Unused committed capacity accrues as "burst credits" that can be used by customer next 60 days. If not used, credits expire or Redwood reallocates capacity to others after window.
  - Pros: customer feels less risky; Redwood recovers value of unused hours by reassigning after short window
  - Cons: bookkeeping complexity; possible negative perception if credits expire
  - Example mechanics: 1 hour unused = 1 credit. Customer can carry up to 20% of monthly commit as credits. Credits older than 60 days auto-convert to Redwood pool and customer receives small rebate or token for future purchases.

Scenario D: Hybrid commitment with utilization floors and true-ups
  - Contract sets a monthly committed capacity and a utilization floor (e.g., 50%). If actual utilization < floor, customer pays a minimum charge to Redwood (true-up). If utilization > committed, customer pays overage at a pre-specified overage rate (lower than on-demand).
  - Pros: protects Redwood margin; predictable revenue cadence for infra planning
  - Cons: customers dislike floors; requires good sales negotiation and pre-sales modeling
  - Example: committed price $10.00; utilization floor 50% => minimum monthly charge = committed_hours * 0.5 * $10.00

Blended-rate model (detailed idea):
- Sell "Committed Units" where 1 Unit = 1 A100-equivalent-hour. When serving, runtime reports fractional consumption by model and kernel; billing uses a conversion table mapping actual host hardware to Unit consumption (e.g., RTX-6000 = 0.7 Unit-hour when running equivalent workload).
- Periodic reconciliation: monthly report shows per-host utilization and conversion factors used. If conversion gives customer advantage (lower cost than target), Redwood still honors committed price; if conversion results in higher effective cost, apply small adjustment or cap at committed price to avoid customer churn for first 3 months.
- Key operational needs: accurate kernel/throughput benchmarks by family, telemetry hooks in serving runtime to attribute execution to host SKU.

Packing and Utilization policies (ops requirements):
- Default packing: place committed workloads on dedicated-capacity-qualified hosts; when utilization below 70% across pool, Redwood can temporarily co-locate compatible non-committed workloads (best-effort) up to a soft cap (e.g., 20% of pool).*
- Eviction: non-committed workloads should be preempted with >30s notice when committed customer needs scale.
- Monitoring: per-commit pool dashboard showing 5/30/90 day effective utilization, burst-credit balance, and 95th percentile latency by model.

Questions / open tradeoffs (for finance + sales):
- What is acceptable maximum customer-visible price opacity for blended pools? Sales feedback needed.
- How to model worst-case margin if committed customers primarily use low-utilization patterns (long context, small QPS)? Add model-level multipliers to forecast tokens per GPU-hour.
- How many months of credits should be allowed? 1 month gives more elasticity to customers but reduces Redwood’s ability to re-sell capacity. 3 months is generous but risky.
- Should we offer a convertible commit that can be partly redeemed as higher-grade GPU access (tiered upgrades)? How to price conversion?

Modeling checklist for next steps (deliverables for finance + pricing team):
- Build a simple spreadsheet that calculates per-commit effective $/token under each scenario A-D using inputs: commit_hours, expected_utilization_curve (hourly), avg_model_profile (tokens/hour), hardware_mix probabilities, term, discount rate for upfront.
- Add columns for worst-case (40% util), median (60%), best (85%) and compute Redwood gross margin for each.
- Simulate 500 random customer profiles (mix of bursty vs steady) to estimate tail risk and required headroom.
- Produce customer-facing one-pager with 2 simple examples (startup: 8 GPUs monthly commit, enterprise: 128 GPUs annual commit) showing cost and flexibility differences.

Notes to self / sales talking points (raw):
- "Blended units simplify buying: you buy capacity, not nodes. We guarantee latency SLOs for models we certify on each family."
- "Monthly commit + burst credits is a low-friction first step — customers can buy into predictability without locking a year."

Appendix: rough example calculation (monthly commit example)
Inputs:
- Customer commits: 10 A100-equivalent GPUs for 30 days (720 hours) -> committed hours = 7,200
- Committed price (scenario B blended): $10.20 / hour -> monthly cost = 7,200 * 10.20 = $73,440
- If realized average utilization = 60% -> effective used hours = 4,320 -> effective $/used-hour = $73,440 / 4,320 = $17.00 / used-hour (customer perspective)
- Expressed as $/M tokens (anchor 100M tokens/hour): $17.00 / 100M tokens = $0.17 / 1M tokens -> helpful to show to customers as $/1M tokens rather than $/GPU-hour

Endnotes / links to reference tables we should include in spreadsheet:
- conversion factors by SKU (placeholder): A100=1.0, A800=0.95, RTX-6000=0.68
- example kernel throughput table (we will replace with real bench results from applied-ml team)

Historical context / why different from previous docs:
- This doc focuses on customer-facing commit primitives and how to express them (units/credits/blended) rather than sensitivity matrices. Aim is to produce a tangible set of experimentable pricing offers.

Feedback welcome — if you’re picking this up, add notes inline or drop a Slack thread in #pricing with subject "dedicated commit playbook".
